summary_html: CPS **accepts** a report for **investigation/assessment**. CAPTA sets the floor for investigation procedures; CFSR evaluates timeliness, safety, and decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — investigation standards tied to funding  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — timeliness & response conformity indicators

primary_citations.citation_text: District of Columbia - D.C. Code Title 4, Chapter 13, Subchapter I, Part A (Reporting Abuse and Neglect) — §§ 4-1301.04, 4-1301.06 investigation and findings
District of Columbia - D.C. Code Title 16, Chapter 23, Subchapter I (Proceedings Regarding Delinquency, Neglect, or Need of Supervision)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: When CPS receives a report identifying particular children as abused, the Child Abuse Prevention Act creates a special relationship imposing on the District a duty to take the steps the Act prescribes for those children, so summary judgment for the District was error.
key_cases.relevance: It defines the investigative conduct the Child Abuse Prevention Act required once a report was accepted.
key_cases.quote: From that moment on, the District had a duty to take certain steps prescribed by the Act for the protection of those children.

key_cases.case_name: V.K. v. Child & Family Services Agency
key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: On judicial review of a CFSA administrative decision upholding a 'substantiated' abuse entry in the Child Protection Register, CFSA bears the burden by a preponderance at the fair hearing and the court will disturb the hearing officer's finding only if the record compels a contrary conclusion; the decision was affirmed on substantial evidence.
key_cases.relevance: It describes the evidentiary record, including hearsay, on which CFSA investigations are sustained.
key_cases.quote: At the hearing, CFSA bore the burden of proof by a preponderance of the evidence.

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: Probable cause supported the medical hold and shelter care of an infant with suspected shaken baby syndrome and the parents' Child Protection Register listing did not violate due process, but the warrantless seizure of the sibling from inside the family home was remanded for a determination whether exigent circumstances existed.
key_cases.relevance: It addresses how far CFSA may go during an in-depth investigation before a court order is required.
key_cases.quote: under the Fourth Amendment, a lawful seizure of children from their parents' custody requires a court order, e.g., a warrant, probable cause, or exigent circumstances

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: The Improved Child Abuse Investigations Amendment Act of 2002 does not bar Superior Court judges from admitting the results of court-ordered mental evaluations in neglect hearings, such examinations under D.C. Code § 16-2315(e)(4) are not shielded by the doctor-patient privilege, and the neglect adjudication was supported by sufficient evidence.
key_cases.relevance: It resolves what evaluation evidence gathered during the assessment phase may be used against a parent.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the trial court's neglect adjudication was supported by sufficient evidence

timeline_requirements.deadline: Within 24 hours of the start of the investigation
45 days for the full investigation (60 days in the listed cases); final report within 5 business days after completion
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of the first notice of the suspected abuse or neglect
